transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I guess what finally got me to come in is this thing with bridges—high bridges, specifically. I keep planning my whole day around not having to drive over them. Like I’ll take the long way, leave earlier, all that. Which is funny because in HR I’m always telling people to be practical and not overcomplicate things, and then here I am adding twenty minutes to avoid one stretch of road.

And if I can’t avoid it, I get through it, but I’m gripping the wheel so tight my hands hurt. Just kind of white-knuckling it the whole way until I’m off the bridge.
When you’re on a high bridge, what is the thing you’re most afraid will happen?

It’s mostly… I know it sounds ridiculous, because those bridges over the bay are built fine. I know people drive over them all day long and nothing happens. But when I get near one, my head just goes straight to, like, what if the car goes right over the side?

And then I’ll think about the railing, the drop, all that. I mean, I used to drive that way years ago without making such a production of it—my brother lives out that direction, and we’d go for cookouts and everything—but now my mind just treats it like it’s not safe, even though I know it is.
Do these sudden rushes of fear ever happen when you’re not on or approaching a high bridge?

Not really out of the blue, no. It’s pretty tied to seeing the bridge or knowing I’m coming up on it. Like as soon as I see it ahead, my chest gets tight, my hands start sweating on the wheel, and I kind of lock in—stare straight ahead like, okay, just get to the other side.

It’s strange because I can sit in traffic other places and be annoyed, sure, but not like that. It’s that bridge coming into view that sets it off.
